name: Cursor for Kids
contribution: A friendly web app that teaches kids how to use Cursor safely and creatively.
headline: Teach kids to build with AI — by asking, reading, and remixing
summary: Cursor for Kids is a small, offline-friendly playground that walks 8–12 year olds through their first AI-assisted project. Kids pick something to build, the app helps them write a great prompt for Cursor, explains the code in plain language, and reminds them of safety rules along the way.
body:
Most kids meet AI the wrong way: they type 'make game', paste whatever comes back, and learn nothing. Cursor for Kids flips that on its head. It treats Cursor like a workshop tool: useful, powerful, and worth respecting.

The app has seven starter projects — quiz game, pet name generator, calculator, story generator, hobby webpage, snake game, and a friendly chatbot. Each one comes with a six-step guide: what to build, describe it clearly, ask Cursor, read the code, change one thing, and debug when it breaks.

The main feature is the Prompt Builder. Kids fill in a few kid-sized form fields (what, theme, features, tools) and watch a clear prompt assemble in real time, ready to copy into Cursor. A 'Good vs Bad prompts' gallery shows side-by-side examples so kids can see exactly what makes a prompt clearer.

'Explain Like I'm 10' lets kids paste any HTML, CSS, or JavaScript and get plain-English explanations of what each piece does, what they can change, and what might break — all powered by a tiny rule-based analyzer that runs entirely on the device. No code is ever sent over the network.

The AI Safety Rules section covers the things grown-ups forget to mention: don't share personal info, don't copy code you don't understand, AI can make mistakes, use AI to learn — not to cheat. Kids tap each rule when they understand it, earning a Safety Star saved in their browser. Eight Cursor Practice Cards round it out with copy-ready prompts for explaining a file, fixing an error, adding a feature, and asking Cursor for a plan before any code is written.

The whole thing is a Next.js static site hosted on GitHub Pages with no backend, no accounts, and no tracking — built so a parent, teacher, or curious kid can open it on any device and start learning straight away.
